sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## What this repository is

`theta-agent` — a **pi package** (extensions + skills for the [pi](https://pi.dev) coding agent) that grows into **Theta**, a science co-researcher agent for biology/biomedicine. It is the code repo of the Theta campaign; design decisions (T1–T10), milestone definitions, and task handoffs live in the campaign vault (path in `CLAUDE.local.md`). Treat the vault as read-only reference.

Current state: 0.5.0 — M5 is shipped. The M1 base ships the `theta` launcher (a thin `bin/theta.mjs` that runs `pi -e <package-root>`; macOS/Linux — Windows waits for M8, tracked in issue #2) and the Tier-1 library: K-Dense skills vendored verbatim per ADR 0001 plus the self-authored `theta-research-loop` orchestrator, with re-syncs at milestone boundaries (`docs/agents/resync.md`). M2 adds the first connector skill, `theta-lit-search` (PubMed, arXiv, Semantic Scholar), landed tracer-first: search and get-by-identifier with pacing, in-200 error detection, and credential redaction enforced in its scripts (ADR 0002; script invariants in `docs/agents/connector-scripts.md`). M3 adds `theta-notebook`, the project notebook skill (ADR 0003): five dated provenance-entry types with content-addressed, graded evidence snapshots under the research project's `.theta/`, a recorder script under the connector-script invariants, a notebook-written attestation in the dogfood auditor, and orchestrator doctrine weaving recording into all six loop stages. M4 ships the compute gateway `theta-compute` (ADR 0004) from `gateway/` — a FastMCP server wrapping the Slurm CLI with argv arrays only, bearer auth from deploy-time env, one audit JSONL line per tool call, and the seven generic tools (the read-only environments/status pair plus the stage–submit–logs–cancel–fetch lifecycle) behind the path sandbox and the command guard, plus the typed `run_alphafold3` rendering the deploy-time template registry's registered template with its free variables only — all out of the npm tarball. On the theta side, M4 landed the gateway skill's lifecycle doctrine and the submit gate (#54), and the notebook's job-record path (#55): a compute run records a method entry whose evidence item is the assembled gateway job record, graded `re-executed` when its artifacts were fetched, and the orchestrator's execute stage routes cluster jobs to `theta-compute`. M5 stacks the safety gates: the deploy-time submit capability (ADR 0006) and the per-principal submit ceiling on the gateway, and on the theta side the submit gate grown into the stacked gate framework (#95) — the literal three-tool confirm set pinned against the gateway's destructive annotations (disagreement is drift and refuses loudly), concurrency-safe stacked confirms (pi 1.4.0's concurrent-dialog fix is the floor), `parentToolCallId` riding prompts, refusals, and the session-dir gate log (`gate.jsonl`, one JSONL line per gated decision), and the dogfood auditor reading codemode's `nestedCalls` records instead of assuming a flat call sequence. M5 S3 (#96) makes the rig itself gateway-bearing: the clean-room rig admits the gateway token as its second credential (`--gateway`, URL host rewritten to the Docker host alias, preflighted in-container before launch — the token rides a 0600 env file, never argv), a checked-in RPC confirm driver (`test/rig/rpc-driver.mjs`) answers the submit gate for headless `--rpc` evidence legs, the gateway skill carries the capability/throttle/codemode doctrine, the auditor finds the transcript by its own name grammar beside the gate log, and the M5 dogfood (gated submit with confirm, held refusal, throttle) ran in the rig against the live gateway. M6 opens the eval suite (ADR 0007) with the replay net's tracer (#133): a checked-in scenario list (`test/eval/scenarios.mjs`), the typed normalization layer with its five rewrite classes, and one connector fixture — a sanitized rig capture — pinned three ways in the keyless standard suite (provenance: one digest per model-visible surface class, so a model-visible edit reds until a fresh capture; snapshot: the normalized entry tree equals its committed snapshot; determinism: pi's reconstruction yields one context hash), with the capture pipeline (`test/eval/capture.mjs`) and doctrine in `docs/agents/eval.md` — all outside the npm tarball.

## pi-package rules

- Host-provided packages (`@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`, `@earendil-works/pi-ai`, `@earendil-works/pi-agent-core`, `@earendil-works/pi-tui`, `typebox`) go in `peerDependencies` with `"*"` ranges — never `dependencies`, never bundled.
- Keep the `pi-package` keyword (gallery eligibility) and the explicit `pi` manifest (`extensions`, `skills`) in `package.json`. Manifest fields are arrays of strings — pi silently drops bare-string fields (guarded by `test/manifest.test.mjs`).
- Never install `pi-mcp-adapter` — an installed adapter replaces pi's built-in MCP support (native since pi 0.99).
- Target pi ≥ 1.4.0 and Node ≥ 22.19.0. The floor moves only at milestone boundaries, under the standing adoption rule recorded on #87 — a held review is recorded on the parent spec, never silent. Package loading uses `pi -e <source>`; local-path sources load without copying, so a repo checkout works exactly like the installed package.
- The pi extension API is read from the installed package, not the web — the paths below sit under the pi install root (`$(npm root -g)/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/`): `docs/extensions.md` (events, the tool-call pipeline, UI modes), `docs/mcp.md` (tool naming and exposure — MCP tool names are sanitized to `[A-Za-z0-9_]`, so a server hyphen registers as an underscore), and `dist/core/extensions/types.d.ts` for the exact event and context shapes.

## Conventions

- Conventional commits (`feat:`, `chore:`, `docs:`). Tabs and existing field order in `package.json`.
- Extract a shared helper as soon as the same logic shape appears twice — tree-wide, not per-module: a module boundary created mid-strike is where duplication is born, so the shared shape gets one home before the second caller (tests included). Copying code verbatim is for separately shipped trees only — skill-to-skill, never within a file.
- Failure paths in runner and helper scripts: child-process spawns inherit the environment (overlay onto `process.env`, never replace it — the eslint `spawn-env-inherit` rule enforces direct call sites); `finally` cleanup never masks the primary failure; a machine-readable result lands as a file when its channel is shared with payload output (the exit-status rule — and a pipeline whose exit gates the next step runs unpiped or under `set -o pipefail`: a `tee` or `tail` in the tail position reports its own status, and #117's failed cluster re-deploy sailed through an `&&` chain that way).
- An accepted behavior delta — ordering, precedence, message bytes — is pinned by a test in the same strike; the PR body discloses what the suite already owns (#113's read-precedence delta reached the merge round disclosed but unpinned, and the merge round paid the pin).
- The review round names every accepted deviation from the spec's letter — additions beyond the enumeration included — with the reason; the disclosure lands in the same strike's PR body, not in a later pass (#127's survey-inputs bullet rode through PR #128's draft review undisclosed, and the triage round paid the disclosure).
- An extraction test — one that pulls structured tokens out of prose — consumes from its anchor: the match opens the claim it pins, leading whitespace only, never searching forward past other text. An unanchored match can borrow a later passage and pass silently (#122's review round caught the prose check's enumeration doing exactly that).
- A spec's acceptance numbers and failure-mode claims are measured before the spec lands — a claim one command can falsify is a delta the strike inherits for free (#120's lint:dups "count drops" claim was false at min-tokens 50: the four mirrors were never token-level clones, and the strike paid the probes to falsify it).
- Secrets ride files — a read-only mount or a `--env-file` — into child processes and containers. An argv element is process-table-visible, so no credential, token, or header value rides one (the M5 S3 review round caught the gateway token on a `docker exec -e`; the preflight env file is the shape).
- When a change supersedes text in a steering doc (`CLAUDE.md`, `GLOSSARY.md`, `docs/adr/`), the same strike edits that text — and superseded means stale by omission as well as false: a section that describes the changed surface covers the new behavior in the same strike (S1's ceiling paragraph was omission-stale through three review passes; only a post-merge strike fixed it).
- A strike that changes a self-authored skill's `SKILL.md` bumps that skill's frontmatter `version:` in the same strike — the field is the skill's own minor, not the package's.
- `.npmrc` pins the official registry (the machine default is npmmirror).
- PR bodies, repo prose, and committed fixtures are public surfaces: cluster account names, SSH aliases, and node names never enter them — they live in `CLAUDE.local.md`, and GitHub keeps body edit history, so a scrub-after is not undo. A committed fixture is the sharpest case — a captured transcript above all: sanitization redacts the payload its tool outputs carry (node lists, job names), not only machine paths; the S2 codemode fixture shipped node lists until a round-2 review caught them. The recipe lives with the golden fixtures in `test/dogfood-audit.test.mjs`. (The cluster's own name is public — ADR 0004 names it.) The Spec review checks.
- No build step; tests use Node's built-in node:test runner (pi loads extension TS via jiti). Verify changes with `npm test`, `npm run lint`, `npm run lint:py` (ruff over the self-authored skill scripts and the gateway tree — vendored trees stay verbatim and out of scope), `npm run lint:sh` (pipefail over the repo's shell surfaces; exceptions argue in the lint), `npm run lint:dups` (jscpd duplication ratchet), and `npm run typecheck`; check shipped files with `npm pack --dry-run`.
- Commits run the suite via the versioned `.githooks/pre-commit` hook; enable it per clone with `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`.
- Dogfood acceptance criteria are met on captured evidence — session transcripts for the skill criteria, recorded exit status and stderr for clean boot — never the model's self-report. Procedure: `docs/agents/dogfood.md`. Dogfood and adversarial sessions run in the clean-room rig (`test/rig/`, ADR 0005): `node test/rig/run.mjs run "<prompt>"`; the provider key and — on a `--gateway` leg — the gateway token are the only credentials that enter it (the cluster SSH key never does; the container reaches the gateway through the host-side port-forward, preflighted in-container before launch), and a gated headless leg runs `--gateway --rpc` — the checked-in confirm driver answers the submit gate.

## Git workflow — one "coding strike" per task

1. Start the strike in a new git worktree on a feature branch. A worktree inside the repo (`.claude/worktrees/`) resolves the checkout's `node_modules`; one placed elsewhere needs `npm ci` first. Files read before entering the worktree carry the old base — re-read anything you are about to anchor-edit, and fetch `origin main` before diffing against or removing the worktree.
2. On the first commit, open a **draft** PR against `main` and run `node scripts/check-strike.mjs <spec#>` from the strike worktree: the evidence leg passes by design at draft time, and the CI leg still exits 1 while a check runs pending — the printed offender line, not the exit code, tells pending from a real failure. The child walk is the draft-time signal: a gate defect or a missing child surfaces with the strike ahead of it, not at ready time (S1's gate read a blocked-by mention as an unlanded child; #61 fixed the detection, and the early run keeps the next defect cheap). Run the strike's review round at draft time too, **before any dogfood capture**: the reviewer sees the diff with the least context pressure, its fixes land while the tree is cheap to change, and the evidence pair then captures once at the final HEAD. The reverse order pays a full recapture every time a review fix moves HEAD — M5 S3 and S4 each paid one on 2026-10-31 (three live legs with cluster toggles; the closeout pair), review-first would have paid neither. Review first, capture once.
3. Commit and push every further change to that PR branch, and refresh the PR body as each strike lands — the body is read mid-flight by reviewers and the owner, not only before ready.
4. Before marking the PR ready, run `node scripts/check-strike.mjs <spec#>` from the strike worktree — every child of the spec issue must be landed on the branch or already closed (a closeout ticket for the post-merge steps is the expected open exception; a childless issue is a maintenance strike). The same gate fails a PR whose body attests dogfood evidence at an SHA that is not HEAD — recapture the pair, never rebind the words — and refuses while any PR check is non-pass, pending included (M3's red `verify` sat four hours past ready; only merge-day habit caught it). Refresh the PR's title and body to cover every landed child, then mark the PR ready and run the review pass over everything changed since the draft round before merging to `main`. For milestone-sized PRs, consider one external-model review round before merge — M2's Codex round caught a defect class two same-model rounds missed.
5. The adversarial loop's stop condition is judgment: once findings require crafted attack strings that honest usage would never produce, stop, record them as a residual trust boundary, and move on. "Findings stay wording-level for two consecutive rounds" applies only to findings a realistic session could trigger; if it has not fired within ~10 rounds, it will not — an adversarial reviewer regenerates findings indefinitely, and "clean" is not a stopping condition it can reach.
6. While a review round is in flight, hold further commits on that branch; when its report arrives, triage against the SHA it reviewed.
7. At teardown, run `node scripts/strike-teardown.mjs <branch>` from anywhere inside the repo — it anchors the main checkout by the shared git dir, refuses unless the branch is merged into `origin/main` (the guard that licenses the `-D`, since plain `-d` compares against the lagging remote topic branch), pulls `main` fast-forward, removes the worktree, and deletes the branch last: the worktree holds it checked out, so the delete refuses until the worktree is gone. A harness-created worktree carries the session's own lock — exit it through the harness's worktree-exit tool before the teardown, or the remove refuses on the lock (the M5 S0 retro). A manual teardown repeats that order with every git command anchored to the main checkout (`git -C <main-checkout>`) — a command run inside the worktree acts on the feature branch (the S4 retro's stray pull fast-forwarded it; the S5 retro repeated the accident), and a session standing in the removed worktree loses its git context (the S3 retro session).

## Publishing

`npm publish` is owner-only (browser 2FA; non-interactive publishes fail with `EOTP`). Prepare the release, commit, push — then stop and let the owner publish. It runs from the repo checkout — the committed `.npmrc` pins `registry.npmjs.org` (the machine default is npmmirror) — and that checkout must be the merged tree first: `git pull --ff-only origin main`, then confirm `package.json`'s version and the `npm pack --dry-run` file count match the release, because the M3 publish ran from a stale checkout (0.2.0, 289 files) and only npm's version-conflict refusal caught it. A publish that fails `E404` before any OTP prompt is a lapsed npmjs token, not a missing package: run `npm login` from inside the repo, then retry.

## Agent skills

### Issue tracker

Issues live in GitHub Issues on `hugolld/theta-agent`, managed with the `gh` CLI. See `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.

### Triage labels

Default five-role vocabulary (each label string equals its role name). See `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`.

### Domain docs

Single-context: root `GLOSSARY.md` + `docs/adr/`. See `docs/agents/domain.md`. Glossary edits are suite-enforced: `_Avoid_` terms are banned from self-authored prose, every headword word must appear in it, a headword outside the provenance grandfather list names its deciding artifact, and an ADR's `(GLOSSARY)` markers match its declared coinages — the scan list lives in `test/skills-library.test.mjs` and verifies itself: self-authored prose (docs, skill text, and the extension sources' user-facing strings, not script comments) that carries glossary vocabulary joins that list in the same strike that lands it, and a file carrying a headword while off the list fails the converse test by name (S1's gateway README caught a banned term the moment it joined; S2's schema doc rode through two reviews until the check existed).

### Connector scripts

Connector helper scripts (`theta-lit-search`, plus the `theta-notebook` recorder) share enforced invariants — exit-code contract, classification shape, repeat-the-call records. See `docs/agents/connector-scripts.md`.

### Compute gateway

`gateway/` holds `theta-compute` (M4, ADR 0004): a FastMCP server wrapping the Slurm CLI, out of the npm tarball and out of Python lint's blind spot. Institutional facts ride deploy-time env; the audit-line shape, ALLOW/DENY/HOLD/THROTTLE semantics, and the phase-0 deploy recipe live in `gateway/README.md`. The deploy-time submit capability (M5, ADR 0006) is the outer bound on job creation: while off — the cluster-side `theta-compute.env`, sourced by every start line — the job-creating tools answer a hard HOLD refusal and the observed state rides every mutating audit line. Inside it, the per-principal submit ceiling (M5 S1) bounds runaway submits: past the deploy-env ceiling (default 20 per rolling hour, the count derived from the audit log itself) the same tools answer a THROTTLE refusal naming the principal, the count, and the window. Inside those server bounds, the theta-side submit gate stays the inner per-call gate — since M5 S2 the stacked gate framework (`extensions/submit-gate.ts`), whose three-tool confirm set is pinned against the gateway's annotations (a disagreement refuses as drift) and whose gate log (`gate.jsonl`) rides the session dir with `parentToolCallId` on nested calls. The offline tests drive the tools at the MCP boundary against the stub Slurm binaries in `test/fixtures/gateway/bin/`. A live step blocked on the cluster path parks — one scheduled re-probe, never a retry loop (waiting over one live connection is not retrying) — and resumes from the parked step when the path returns.

### Replay net

`test/eval/` holds the eval suite's base layer (M6, ADR 0007): the replay net, keyless and deterministic in the standard suite. A checked-in scenario list is the only source of capture prompts; `test/eval/capture.mjs` drives the rig and lands sanitized fixtures (one per scenario) with a provenance manifest — one digest per model-visible surface class — and a normalized snapshot; the net replays each fixture through pi's public reconstruction exports and holds the three pins (provenance, snapshot, determinism). A model-visible change lands only with a fresh eval capture — a red provenance pin names the stale fixture; never edit a fixture or snapshot by hand. Doctrine, the digest-scope decision, and the drill-leg recipe: `docs/agents/eval.md`.

### SKILL.md frontmatter

Descriptions are capped at 1..1024 chars and must stay plain-scalar-safe (no `: ` sequences in the value). `test/skills-library.test.mjs` enforces both: it parses frontmatter with the `yaml` package — the same engine pi runs — so invalid YAML fails the suite instead of pi silently dropping the skill.

</project_instructions>

# Theta literature search

A Theta-owned connector skill: one script per scholarly source, with the
API's contract enforced in code the model calls. PubMed, arXiv, and
Semantic Scholar ship in this slice set. This skill owns **search** and
**get-by-identifier** for its sources — read-only metadata with
provenance, never full text or citation graphs.

## Division of labor with paper-lookup

The vendored `paper-lookup` skill stays the general scholarly interface for
its 18 databases. This skill takes over only the sources it connects:

| Intent | Route to |
|---|---|
| Search biomedical literature by topic or query | `theta-lit-search` (PubMed) |
| Exact metadata for a PMID you already hold | `theta-lit-search` (PubMed) |
| Search arXiv for quantitative-bio, math, or CS methods work | `theta-lit-search` (arXiv) |
| Exact metadata for an arXiv ID you already hold | `theta-lit-search` (arXiv) |
| Search across fields with citation counts (Semantic Scholar) | `theta-lit-search` (Semantic Scholar) |
| Exact metadata for a DOI you already hold | `theta-lit-search` (Semantic Scholar) |
| Full text, citation graphs, preprint servers, Crossref, OpenAlex, Europe PMC, everything else | `paper-lookup` |

Routing is stable by design: as later milestones add sources, they extend
this skill's table; the general interface never loses coverage to it.

## Why the script, not curl

All three connected APIs fail *inside* HTTP 200 bodies and pace their
callers (neither failure is visible on the status line); PubMed takes its
API key in the query string and Semantic Scholar in a request header. The
bundled scripts enforce all of it in code:

- **Pacing**: a monotonic-clock floor between calls — PubMed at most 3
  requests/second anonymous, 10 with a key; arXiv one request every three
  seconds, single connection (a Terms-of-Use ceiling that applies to every
  machine you control, not to one process); Semantic Scholar one
  request/second with a key (the introductory keyed rate).
- **In-200 errors**: a PubMed 200 body carrying `{"error": ...}`, an arXiv
  200 feed whose single entry is titled `Error` (a shape that reads as a
  successful one-hit search), and a Semantic Scholar 200 body carrying
  `{"error": ...}` each surface as a non-zero exit, never as a confident
  result. arXiv's throttle is a bare plain-text body, not XML, and
  Semantic Scholar's is a `{"message", "code"}` body; each script
  recognizes its throttle whatever the HTTP status.
- **Redaction**: `api_key`, `email`, and `tool` values never appear in the
  provenance the scripts echo; the Semantic Scholar key rides in the
  `x-api-key` header and only the header name survives into provenance.
  Parameter names survive so a reader can repeat the call with their own
  key.

Calling NCBI, export.arxiv.org, or api.semanticscholar.org directly with
curl re-introduces every hazard the scripts exist to remove. Do not.

## Operations

```bash
# PubMed search: query -> bounded list of records with provenance
python3 scripts/pubmed.py --query "CRISPR gene therapy" [--retmax 8] [--sort pub_date] [--json]

# Get by identifier: PMID -> exact metadata summary
python3 scripts/pubmed.py --pmid 34567890 [--json]

# arXiv search: query -> bounded list of records with provenance
python3 scripts/arxiv.py --query "ti:attention AND cat:cs.CL" [--retmax 8] [--sort submittedDate] [--order ascending] [--json]

# Get by identifier: arXiv ID -> exact metadata summary
python3 scripts/arxiv.py --arxiv-id 1706.03762 [--json]

# Semantic Scholar search: query -> bounded list of records with citation counts
python3 scripts/semanticscholar.py --query "crispr off-target" [--retmax 8] [--json]

# Get by identifier: DOI -> exact metadata summary
python3 scripts/semanticscholar.py --doi 10.1038/s41587-024-02123-4 [--json]
```

Requires Python 3.11+ (standard library only). If `python3` is older, run
`python3.13`, `python3.12`, or `python3.11` — the scripts name them when the
gate trips. `--retmax` caps results at 1..200 (default 8) on PubMed and
arXiv, and at 1..100 on Semantic Scholar (the API's relevance-search
ceiling). PubMed `--sort` accepts `relevance` (default), `pub_date`,
`Author`, `JournalName`; arXiv `--sort` accepts `relevance` (default),
`submittedDate`, `lastUpdatedDate`, with `--order` `ascending` or
`descending` (default `descending`). Semantic Scholar search takes no sort
— relevance is the endpoint's only order. `--pmid` and `--arxiv-id` accept
a comma-separated list, also capped at 200; `--doi` takes exactly one bare
DOI.

Default output is one line per paper —
`title | authors | year | journal | PMID x | DOI y` on PubMed,
`title | authors | year | cat c | arXiv id | DOI y` on arXiv,
`title | authors | year | venue v | cited by n | DOI y` on Semantic
Scholar — then a count line and a provenance line (endpoint URLs with
credentials redacted, access date). `--json` prints the structured records
and provenance instead.

## Exit codes

The exit code is the contract — branch on it, never on the presence of
output:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Success. Zero results included: reported as an explicit empty answer, not an error. On arXiv an unknown identifier is also a zero-result answer; on Semantic Scholar an unknown DOI is too (its documented 404 not-found body). |
| 1 | Usage error — bad arguments, out-of-range values. |
| 2 | Transport failure — network error or non-200 HTTP status. |
| 3 | API error inside an HTTP 200 body — the response lied about succeeding. |
| 4 | Throttled — NCBI's rate-limit error body, arXiv's plain-text `Rate exceeded.`, Semantic Scholar's 429 message body. Wait before retrying; do not hammer. |
| 5 | Credentials unusable (Semantic Scholar only) — no `S2_API_KEY` in the environment, or the key was rejected with HTTP 403. The message carries the key-request URL; relay it so the user can unlock the source in minutes. |

## Credentials

`NCBI_API_KEY` is optional and read from the environment. Without it the
PubMed script runs at the anonymous 3 requests/second and still works — a
fresh install with no keys is useful immediately. A key raises the pace to
10 requests/second (self-service:
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/account/settings/). Never echo the key; the
script already keeps it out of provenance.

arXiv takes no credentials at all: there is no key mechanism and no higher
tier to request. The one-request-per-three-seconds pace is the whole
contract, and the script enforces it.

`S2_API_KEY` is **required** for Semantic Scholar and read from the
environment. The anonymous tier is a rate pool shared among all
unauthenticated users — a first keyless request can already be refused — so
the script never attempts it: without the key it exits 5 before any
request, with the key-request URL in the message. The key is self-service
(https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/api#api-key-form) and arrives by
email; a key buys the deterministic 1 request/second pace. Never echo the
key; the script already keeps it out of provenance (only the `x-api-key`
header name appears, value redacted).

## Output discipline

- Report the total match count alongside the bounded list you show — 8 of
  4,532 is a different claim than 8.
- Carry Semantic Scholar citation counts into the answer — they are the
  source's distinctive free metadata (`influential_citation_count` rides
  along in `--json`).
- Semantic Scholar queries are plain text with no special syntax, and
  hyphenated terms yield no matches: replace hyphens with spaces when
  composing the query.
- Carry provenance into the answer: endpoint, parameters, access date.
- A zero-result query is an answer ("not in PubMed", "not in arXiv", "not
  in Semantic Scholar"), not a failure — say it plainly rather than
  widening the query silently.
- On arXiv, check `query_as_executed` against the query you sent: an
  unknown field prefix is silently rewritten to `all:` and the search still
  succeeds — wrong, not failed.
- arXiv results change only at midnight; the manual asks for one call per
  query per day. Do not repeat an identical arXiv query within a day.
- Retain the exit-code meaning when relaying: an in-200 error (3) must reach
  the user as an error, not as an empty result set.

## Boundaries

- Read-only metadata: no full text, no abstracts (beyond what PubMed
  eSummary returns; the arXiv records carry none of the abstract the feed
  provides), no citation graphs, no export. Route those intents to
  `paper-lookup`.
- Pacing is per-invocation: two shells running a connector script in
  parallel can in principle burst past the limit — and arXiv's ceiling is
  fleet-wide, so the burst costs the whole operator. A stateless script
  cannot fix this; serialize connector work instead.
- Endpoint facts, parameter details, and the documented failure shapes live
  in `references/pubmed.md`, `references/arxiv.md`, and
  `references/semantic-scholar.md` — read the source's note before
  non-trivial query construction (date ranges, field tags, sort semantics,
  key provisioning).

# PubMed (NCBI E-utilities)

Endpoint contract facts for `scripts/pubmed.py`. Official sources reviewed
2026-10-11 (contract basis: the script docstring and the repo research note
`docs/research/2026-10-11-m2-literature-api-contracts.md`, which also holds
the delta review against the vendored paper-lookup reference).

## Base URL

All requests: `https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/` (NBK25497).

## Authentication

- No key required: anonymous access works at 3 requests/second, so a fresh
  install with no credentials is useful immediately.
- `NCBI_API_KEY` in the environment raises the pace to 10 requests/second.
  Key provisioning is self-service from the NCBI account Settings page
  (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/account/settings/); only one key per
  account, and requesting a new key invalidates the old one.
- The key is passed as the `api_key` query parameter. The script redacts its
  value from every URL and parameter map it echoes.
- `tool` and `email` parameters are deliberately not sent: NCBI states these
  values must be *registered* with them (by email) to satisfy the usage
  policy — merely sending unregistered values adds nothing.

## Endpoints in use

### esearch.fcgi — query to PMIDs

Parameters the script sets: `db=pubmed`, `term`, `retmode=json`,
`retmax` (1..200; API ceiling 10,000), optional `sort`.

- `sort` values: `relevance` (default, "Best Match"), `pub_date`
  (descending), `Author` (ascending first author), `JournalName`.
- Date limits (add to `term` yourself, or extend the script when needed):
  `mindate`/`maxdate` must be used together with `datetype`
  (`pdat`/`mdat`/`edat`); formats `YYYY/MM/DD`, `YYYY/MM`, `YYYY`;
  `reldate` = last n days.
- PubMed hard ceiling: ESearch can only retrieve the first 10,000 records
  matching a query; beyond that, NCBI's answer is date-partitioned queries
  or EDirect — not a bigger retmax.

### esummary.fcgi — document summaries

Parameters: `db=pubmed`, `id` (comma-separated UID list), `retmode=json`.
Returns `result.uids` plus one map per PMID. Record extraction: `title`,
`authors[].name`, `pubdate`/`epubdate`, `fulljournalname`/`source`,
`articleids` (`doi`, `pubmed`).

- Above about 200 UIDs NCBI asks for HTTP POST; the script caps at 200 and
  stays on GET.
- A per-UID error (`{"error": "cannot get document summary", "uid": ...}`)
  arrives inside an otherwise successful HTTP 200 body. The script exits 3.

## Rate limits and pacing

- 3 requests/second anonymous (per IP), 10 with an API key (per key).
- The script enforces a monotonic-clock floor between calls: 0.34 s
  anonymous, 0.11 s keyed — just under the published ceilings, never equal.
- NCBI's timing guidance: large jobs belong on weekends or 9 PM–5 AM
  Eastern on weekdays; violations can get an IP blocked.
- Anonymous responses carry `x-ratelimit-limit` / `x-ratelimit-remaining`
  headers (live-observed 2026-10-11, absent from the Bookshelf; semantics
  unverified). The transport treats a reported `remaining: 0` as an
  advisory 1-second pause — never a skipped call.

## Error format

- **The documented error channel is the body, not the status line.** The
  Bookshelf chapters state no HTTP status for E-utility errors; the
  documented rate-limit failure is
  `{"error": "API rate limit exceeded", "count": "11"}` inside an otherwise
  normal response. Do not branch on status codes for E-utility errors.
- The script classifies every response body: a top-level `error` key, a
  per-UID error, a non-JSON body, or a missing `esearchresult`/`result`
  shape each surface as an error exit — never as a sparse success.

## The connector script

```bash
python3 scripts/pubmed.py --query "CRISPR gene therapy" [--retmax 8] [--sort pub_date] [--json]
python3 scripts/pubmed.py --pmid 34567890 [--json]
```

Exit codes: 0 success (zero results included), 1 usage, 2 transport
(non-200 status or network), 3 API error inside HTTP 200, 4 throttled.

Offline testing: set `THETA_LIT_SEARCH_FIXTURES` to a directory of recorded
bodies consumed in call order (a first line `# status: NNN` encodes a
non-200 status); the transport swap is the whole difference between test
and live. Contract tests: `test/lit-search-pubmed.test.mjs` in the repo.

## Residual

Pacing is per-invocation: parallel shells running the script can in
principle burst past the limit. Serialize PubMed work; a stateless script
cannot fix this.

## Official sources reviewed 2026-10-11

- NCBI Bookshelf, Entrez Programming Utilities Help — "A General
  Introduction to the E-utilities" (NBK25497): base URL, rate limits, API
  key policy, tool/email registration, error message.
- NCBI Bookshelf — "The E-utilities In-Depth: Parameters, Syntax and More"
  (NBK25499): JSON retmode, retmax ceiling, sort values, date parameters,
  POST guidance.
